A review of subjective evaluation, physiological indicators and
cognitive performance in indoor light environment: The role of
illuminance and correlated color temperature
Chao Liua,b, Jiaxin Lia, Xuening Wangb,*, Qiuyun Zangb, Wenhao Wanga,
Weijun Gaoa,c
aInnovation Institute for Sustainable Maritime Architecture Research and Technology, Qingdao University of Technology, China
bCollege of Architecture and Urban Planning, Qingdao University of Technology, China
cFaculty of Environmental Engineering, The University of Kitakyushu, Kitakyushu, 808-0135, Japan
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: Numerous studies have shown that lighting conditions have a significant impact on people’s
Illuminance satisfaction, health, and performance. With the current interest in healthy lighting gradually
Correlated color temperature increasing, more and more researchers have begun to study the effects of light on comfort,
Task performance cognitive performance, and physiological health. This paper seeks to summarize the effects of
Subjective evaluation lighting conditions on subjective comfort, physiological indicators, and cognitive performance.
Physiological indicators
This review collected studies on the effects of indoor lighting (mainly in schools and offices) on
comfort, cognitive performance, and physiological health from 2000 to the present, with a focus
on the role of illuminance and correlated color temperature. The screening process yielded 122
papers that met the criteria. Firstly, the literature was categorized according to light elements and
briefly introduced in terms of task type and experimental settings. Then, the relationships be-
tween different light environments and subjective comfort, physiological indicators and cognitive
performance were summarized and compared. This paper finds that subjective comfort evalua-
tions improve with higher illuminance and correlated color temperatures. However, this
improvement does not result in a linear increase in visual comfort. Cognitive performance also
appears to improve with higher illuminance and higher correlated color temperature. The human
body produces a range of neurophysiological responses as a result of light, which are charac-
terized by melatonin, skin temperature, heart rate, brain waves, and other physiological in-
dicators. This paper proposed potential research and development directions to address the
limitations of current existing studies. This paper provides theoretical support for improving
people’s visual comfort and cognitive performance, as well as a reference for the design of the
same type of experimental research.
1. Introduction
In recent years, there has been a surge in public awareness of the importance of the lighting environment to overall health and well-
being. The focus of built environment academia has expanded from the impact of lighting on building performance and energy use to

the impact on health, well-being, and comfort [1]. Studies have shown that humans spend approximately 90 % or more of their time
indoors [2], making the impact of lighting conditions on satisfaction with the indoor environment critically important [3,4]. Light is
known to affect visual perception, mood, and physical health. Exposure to adverse light environments can damage visual health, and
overexposure can cause retinal disease and increased eye fatigue [5]. Adverse light environments can also cause mental stress and
psychological problems. Extreme light environments can make people more negative and irritable [6]. It was found that nighttime
exposure to high illuminance and blue-rich white light causes sleep deprivation and disruption of circadian rhythms [7,8]. Long-term
exposure also increases the risk of cancer, diabetes, and other diseases. In contrast, exposure to bright, comfortable light greatly
improves mental health [9,10], subjective alertness [11,12], and physiological rhythms [13,14], and reduces the occurrence of
physiological problems. Current research on light environments involves multiple aspects and cross-cutting areas, covering education
[15–17], health [18–26], psychology [27–32], and urban architectural design [33–41]. This paper focuses on exploring the rela-
tionship between indoor light environments and subjective perception, physiological response, and cognitive performance (see
Tables 1–8).
Visible light enters the human eye and reaches the retina to form vision. People actively evaluate the surrounding light environ-
ments based on their visual perception. The current study mainly quantifies these evaluations through questionnaires. Subjective
evaluations mainly include visual comfort, visual satisfaction, visual fatigue, emotional perception and subjective drowsiness. In
addition, light is important in non-visual effects mediated by ganglion cells (ipRGCs) [42], a third type of photoreceptor cells in the
retina. Through this light-induced effect, light exposure indirectly affects mood, sleep, health, alertness, and cognitive performance.
This involves a range of physiological responses and affects a variety of physiological indicators, including pupil size [43–45], body
temperature [20,34,38,46,47], heart rate [24,48], melatonin [21,49,50], skin conductance [51,52], blood pressure [53,54], salivary
amylase [29], and electroencephalogram (EEG) [55,56]. With the policy and research focus on social efficiency, there has been a
proliferation of studies related to the effects of indoor light environments on student learning efficiency and work task performance.
Cognition is a series of activities regarding information processing (reception, interpretation, organization and extraction) when
people perform mental work [57]. Cognition, as the entire processing cycle of information, can be categorized into five cognitive
abilities: attention, perception, memory, language function, and higher-order cognitive skills [58]. Based on the characteristics of
mental work and cognition, cognitive abilities can be broadly viewed as indicators of learning efficiency and work performance.
Different learning and work tasks rely on different cognitive functions. Typically, experiments rate cognitive performance through task
tests. Among them, attention and memory are the most commonly evaluated factors. It was shown that there are complex correlations
between subjective feelings, physiological indicators and cognitive performance. Significant correlations exist between subjective
perception and cognitive performance, with more comfortable light ratings corresponding to better task performance. Some physi-
ological indicators can also be used to judge cognitive performance.
Many researchers have conducted systematic generalizations involving human comfort [59], cognitive function [58], task per-
formance [39,60], alertness [61], and the effect of light on physiology [25]. Among them, Wu et al. [59] summarized the effects of
sound, light, and heat on overall human comfort. They found that the importance of different environmental perceptions in overall
human comfort is not equal. Wang et al. [58] specifically reviewed the relationship between five cognitive functions, including
attention, perception, memory, language function and higher-order cognitive skills, and indoor environmental quality (IEQ). They
found that there is an effect of IEQ on cognitive performance. However, they did not discuss the relationship between each envi-
ronmental factor and each cognitive function separately. The study by Konstantzos et al. [60] reviewed the relationship between
illuminance, luminance ratio and correlated color temperature(CCT) and task performance and summarized the effects of different
light elements on task performance. However, their study did not categorize and generalize task types. Konstantin et al. [25] made a
connection between the immediate excitation effect of light and changes in objective physiological indicators, and found that body
temperature and heart rate can reliably detect the excitation effect of light on humans. This provided a new method for light envi-
ronment research. It can be seen that the current reviews on light environment and subjective comfort, physiological indicators and
cognitive performance are not comprehensive. In terms of the main body of studies, the scope of the studies is too large and includes
other IEQ factors. In terms of the content of the studies, they are homogenous and lack a systematic review of the effects of light.
Therefore, this study conducted an up-to-date review of the literature. Combination of PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for
Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) and traditional manual review methods were used for co-screening. Indoor places, repre-
sented by classrooms and offices, in which long hours of brain activity are required, have been innovatively selected. Subjective
perception, physiological indicators, and cognitive performance were expanded in specific detail for the effects of illuminance and CCT
in the light environments. The aim is threefold. The first is to summarize conclusions about the effects of indoor light environments on

2. Materials and methods
2.1. Scope of the review
In this paper, we reviewed the primary literature published from 2000 through December 2023 on the effects of light exposure on
subjective perception, physiological indicators, and cognitive performance(The non-visual effects of light exposure on the human body
have only received further attention since the discovery of ganglion cells (ipRGCs) [42], the third type of photoreceptor cells in the
human retina, since 2002 [64]). The Web of Science is a comprehensive database encompassing a wide range of literature. Its robust
analysis capabilities enable the rapid identification of influential papers and the identification of current research trends and areas of
focus. Thus, we undertook an extensive collection of paper data from the Web of Science, specifically focusing on research examining
light’s impact on subjective feelings, physiological indicators, and cognitive performance. These papers were then extracted for
keyword co-occurrence analysis. The aim is to identify the focal point of light index study in the field of light-related research in order
to establish the extent of the light indicators for the subsequent comprehensive review. As shown in Fig. 1, the keyword co-occurrence
analysis indicated that illuminance was the most prevalent keyword among those associated with lighting parameters, followed by
CCT. In addition, indicators related to light environment also include luminance, luminance ratio and glare indicators. However, there
are fewer related studies to systematically summarize and review. Therefore, the scope of our study only includes illuminance and CCT.
2.2. Search strategy and review process
The paper screening process is shown in Fig. 2. Fig. 1 clearly illustrated that illumination and CCT were highly recurring keywords.

Therefore, we concluded that the review papers focused on illuminance and CCT. Then, we enlarged the database using traditional
manual review and PRISMA methods to conduct a comprehensive literature search. The expanded database scope mainly included
ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and Web of Science, followed by PubMed and China National Knowledge Infrastructure. The keyword
search used a combination of I and II terms: (I) “Comfort” or “Satisfaction” or “Fatigue” or “Mood” or “Alertness” or “Physical” or
“Mental” or “Pupil” or " Body temperature” or “Blood pressure” or “Melatonin” or “Electroencephalogram” or “Heart rate” or “Heart
rate variability” or “Learning performance” or “Cognitive performance” or “Task performance " or “Cognitive skills” or “Learning
efficiency” or “Work efficiency” or " Work performance ", and (II) “Light” or “Light environment” or “Illumination” or “Indoor lighting”
or “Illuminance” or “Correlated color temperature”. More than one thousand papers were obtained by conducting an initial search in
the databases using keywords. The process of screening the literature involved multiple aspects, including article title, authors, journal
of publication, year of publication, purpose of the study, study population, inclusion criteria, subjective perception, objective phys-
iological indicators, and cognitive performance. The screening process was done independently by at least two researchers and
adhered to PRISMA. The number of literature was reduced to 155 by manually screening the titles of the literature and eliminating
duplicate entries, daylight-related studies, and studies focusing on daylighting control systems. 39 studies that did not address illu-
minance or CCT were further eliminated by reading the abstracts of the remaining 155 papers. Next, a forward and backward search of
cited or quoted papers was conducted to add 24 relevant papers, increasing the number of papers to 143. The full text of these papers
was then read, evaluated and categorized. A total of 122 experimental studies on the subjective and objective effects of illuminance and
CCT on humans were screened.

Based on the above criteria, a total of 122 eligible studies were selected for review. Fig. 3 mainly presents a collection of screened
studies on the effects of light environment on comfort, health, and cognitive performance since 2000. In the past 20 years, the related
research has increased steadily. Especially since 2014, scholars’ attention to light environment and comfort, health, and performance
has increased significantly, and the number of published papers has reached a new peak. In addition, most studies use a combination of
experiments and questionnaires, while very few studies use only questionnaires.
3. The effect of illuminance on subjective evaluation, physiological indicators and cognitive performance
3.1. The effect of illuminance on subjective evaluation
The effect of light on psychology mainly manifests in perception and emotion. After receiving the light stimulus, the human body
will actively evaluate the surrounding light environment based on visual perception. Current studies mainly employ questionnaires to
quantify subjects’ subjective evaluations. This study included 38 studies on the effect of illuminance on subjective evaluation. The
main summary of the study is shown in Fig. 4. Among them, 11 papers evaluated visual comfort and visual satisfaction, 6 evaluated
visual fatigue, 9 evaluated emotional perception using emotion scale, and 11 evaluated subjective sleepiness using Karolinska som-
nolence scale. The study examined indoor environments such as classrooms and offices. Lighting settings mostly use LED lights, and
some use fluorescent lamps. The lighting is controlled within a reasonable range.
Indoor illuminance usually has a direct impact on human visual perception. Huang et al. [63] investigated the acceptable range of

3.2. The effect of illuminance on physiological indicators
The non-visual biological effect of light on humans will cause a series of physiological parameter changes. This paper includes 36
studies on the effects of illuminance on physiological indicators. The main summary of the study is shown in Fig. 5. Among them, 4
papers tested for pupil diameter,7 for melatonin, 8 for electrocardiogram (ECG), 10 for body temperature, and 7 for EEG. Heart rate
and body temperature are the most commonly used test parameters. Melatonin levels needs to be measured after sampling. EEG is a
current trend in research development, offering significant research opportunities.
In terms of the pupil, light enters the human eye through the pupil to form vision. The pupil controls the amount of light that
reaches the retina thus allowing the eye to adapt to changes in light. The size of the pupil decreases in high illuminance and increases in
contrast. This behavior is also known as pupillary light reflex (PLR) [69]. There are three stimulus responses to pupil diameter: the
pupil light response, the pupil near response, and the psycho-sensory pupil response [70]. Therefore, pupil size varies by light, dis-
tance, arousal stimuli, task demands, emotion, decision making, mental work or cognitive activity [71–74]. Also, studies have
demonstrated that pupil diameters are affected by age and gender [44]. In studies on the effect of light on pupil size, Choi et al. [44]
utilized pupil size to evaluate visual perception of horizontal illuminance in the range of 50–1400lx. They found that pupil size varied
within a mean range of 5.2%–7.4 % when visual perception was neutral. This shows the potential of using pupil size to assess people’s
visual perception. In addition, studies have explored the effect of light metrics such as luminance [75] and glare [76] on the pupil. For
example, relative pupil size was found to be negatively correlated with visual discomfort level [77,78] and glare source brightness
[79]. In a systematic review, Hamedani et al. found that relative pupil size correlated with visual discomfort, vertical illuminance of
the eye, and glare index [76].
Previous studies have shown that higher illuminance levels are associated with greater melatonin inhibition, which decreases
relative to exposure time [54,80]. Although some of the studies did not find a significant effect of illuminance on body temperature
[34,38], some of them showed that in terms of body temperature, evening and nighttime exposure to bright light suppresses the
decrease in core body temperature (CBT) and proximal skin temperature (SKT), but decreases distal SKT [81–84]. Interestingly, light
exposure affects thermoregulation by influencing melatonin and thus thermoregulation [46,47]. An inverse relationship between
melatonin levels and CBT has been demonstrated by the administration of exogenous melatonin [85]. Meanwhile some studies have
found that using bright light exposure at different times of the day resulted in different outcomes [20,86]. Light exposure in the
morning resulted in an earlier increase in CBT along with a more rapid decrease in melatonin concentration. However, studies con-
ducted in the afternoon did not find any effect of light exposure on body temperature.
In terms of heart rate, it is found that exposure to bright light (2800lx) before bed delayed the drops in heart rate by 4 h during rest
compared to dim light (120lx) conditions [87]. Ruger et al. [20] compared the heart rate of subjects exposed to bright light at different
time periods. They found a time-dependent effect of bright light on heart rate. At night, but not during the day, heart rate increased
when exposed to bright light. Smolders et al. [18] explored the effects of different illuminance levels on human physiological arousal.

4. The effect of CCT on subjective evaluation, physiological indicators and cognitive performance
4.1. Effects of CCT on subjective evaluations
The subjective evaluation of indoor CCT mainly includes two aspects: thermal comfort and visual comfort, both of which are
generally rated by a simple 5-level or 7-level Likert scale. A total of 26 studies that consider the influence of CCT on subjective
evaluation are included in this study. The main summary of the study is shown in Fig. 7. Among them, 12 studies focus on the thermal
comfort of CCT, mainly referring to the evaluation of heat perception caused by different CCTs. Additionally, there were 11 studies
focusing on the subjective evaluation of visual comfort and visual satisfaction, mainly referring to the visual perception evaluation
after stimulation by different light source CCTs. Visual fatigue was evaluated in five papers. Emotional scale was used to evaluate
emotion perception in seven papers. The Karolinska Sleepiness Scale was used to evaluate subjective sleepiness in seven studies. The
study examined indoor Spaces in classrooms and offices. Lighting settings mostly use LED lights, and some use fluorescent lamps. The
lighting is under control within reasonable limits.
4.1.1. CCT and thermal comfort
The chromo-thermal hypothesis explains the relationship between color and heat perception effectively. In other words, light or
color with wavelengths mainly towards the red end of the visible spectrum induces a warmer sensation, whereas light or color with
wavelengths mainly towards the blue end induces a cooler sensation. There are two main ways to verify this hypothesis. One is to use a
color lamp or a color object for verification, and the other is to use a light source of different CCTs for verification. However, con-
ducting experiments with colored lights that accurately simulate real-life conditions can be challenging. Therefore, this paper mainly
reviews the use of CCT to verify the chromo-thermal hypothesis.
Golasi et al. [106] proposed that under the condition of achieving the same thermal sensation, the air temperature should be
increased by 1.25 ◦C, 0.46 ◦C and 0.23 ◦C respectively for cold light (11530K), neutral light (4000K) and warm light (1772K). This
indicates that the thermal perception temperature is lower in cool light. Huebner et al. [107] set up a light with a CCT of 2700K or
6500K in the experiment, and conducted a 24-20 ◦C cooling cycle or a 20–24 ◦C heating cycle. The subjects were asked to fill out
questionnaires and the number of times the subjects put on and took off clothes at different temperatures was recorded. The study
found that subjects put on more clothes at a high CCT of 6,500K than they did at a low CCT of 2,700K. This shows that low CCT gives

4.1.2. CCT and visual comfort
CCT significantly affects visual comfort. The study found that visual comfort was poorer at lower CCTs but improved at neutral
CCTs (3300K–5300K) [6,17,111]. By exploring the influence of illuminance and CCT on visual response, Lee et al. [6] found that
lighting conditions with low CCT (3000K) and high illuminance (500lx) would cause glare sensation and visual discomfort. They
recommend a neutral CCT (4000K) for office Spaces 500lx and above. Yang et al. [17] found that a CCT of 4000K contributed more to
visual comfort than illuminance. They believe that a CCT of 4000K provides the best lighting comfort for educational settings. Baniya
et al. [111] found that the relative CCT of 4000K is more comfortable than that of 2700K or 6200K. Similar to illuminance, different
activities exhibit varying preferences for CCT. Numerous studies show that lower CCT can make subjects more comfortable and
relaxed, while higher CCT can make subjects more motivated to perform tasks for longer periods of time [112]. And some studies have
obtained accurate CCT values. For example, the most comfortable CCT when relaxing in the office is 4404K and the most comfortable
CCT when working is 6236K [113]. In bedrooms and living rooms, 3000K is preferred for resting, while 5000K is preferred for reading
[49]. These studies suggest that tasks and work scenarios have an impact on the subjective comfort level of CCT. Thus, the effect of CCT
on visual comfort is not only related to the interaction of illuminance with CCT but also to the choice of application scenario.
In summary, CCT has a significant impact on visual comfort. Different activity scenarios require different optimal CCTs. For
relaxing and resting spaces, a lower CCT (3000K) is recommended, while a neutral CCT (4000K) is suitable for indoor learning or
working environments like classrooms and offices to ensure visual comfort during work and study. On the other hand, a higher CCT
(6500K) can enhance work and study performance without causing visual discomfort. Future research could focus on personalizing
lighting design to meet the requirements of various scenarios.

Studies have shown that AAC increases more at high CCT of 7000K than at low CCT of 3000K. This indicates that the brain is more

increased.

melatonin, alleviates the drop in body temperature during sleep, and increases the heart rate and brain activity. It can be seen that high
CCT can activate the brain and enhance people’s enthusiasm. However, excessively high CCT can also increase stress and stress
response, negatively impacting human health.

attention. However, the effect on attention does not increase linearly with the increase in CCT. Significant correlations were found
between CCT and responsiveness and memory. A large number of studies have shown that under the illuminance of blue-rich white
light with high CCT, students not only show faster cognitive processing speed and reaction speed [13,119], but also have better
performance in memory tasks [120,121]. For example, Hawes et al. [119] found in verbal working memory and spatial working
memory tests that as the CCT increased from 3000K to 6000K, the reaction time of the subjects gradually decreased and the memory
gradually improved. This suggests that higher CCT results in better performance on reactive and memory tasks [95]. However, other
studies have found the exact opposite. Evidence shows that altering CCT has no effect on attention performance or short- and long-term
memory [31,108,122]. This may be due to the effect of exposure time, or it may be because multi-sensory interaction has an impact on
indoor environmental perception. There are interactions between different environmental factors. In terms of executive power, Sun
et al. [27] found that the experimental setting of intermediate CCT (5000K) was more conducive to improving the thinking ability and
executive performance of subjects. Research by Ferlazzo et al. [123] has shown that cold light can improve subjects’ ability to perform
complex tasks. At the same time, studies show that neutral CCT (5000K) is more conducive to improving reading concentration [22,37]
and reading efficiency [65].
In general, increasing CCT is beneficial to improve attention, reflexes, memory and executive ability, so that subjects have better
cognitive performance on task tests. The improvement in working memory and attention can be attributed to the stimulation of the
sympathetic nervous system by bright light [97]. In addition, the higher the CCT, the more significant the inhibition effect on
melatonin. This enhances self-reported alertness, promotes positive emotions, and eliminates fatigue, thereby improving task per-
formance [50]. However, high CCT did not benefit all cognitive performances. A neutral CCT was found to be more conducive to
enhanced thinking, executive skills, and reading efficiency. Therefore, in actual design, considering the enhancement of overall
cognitive performance, a suitable neutral color temperature can be chosen to adjust the indoor lighting environment.
5. Summary and potential research
This systematic review examines the relationship between the light environment and subjective perception, physiological in-
dicators, and cognitive performance in indoor scenes represented by classrooms and offices in existing studies. This review offers
several advantages and contributions. Firstly, the advantage lies in the fact that the scope of this review is targeted to spaces where
mental work is performed indoors, as represented by classrooms and offices. There is more scope for application promotion. Secondly,
the research content is diverse. This study included subjective evaluation, task test and physiological measurement to achieve a
multidimensional assessment of the impact of light on psychology, physiology and performance. In addition, during the article
screening process, at least two researchers completed the various stages of screening. A systematic review was conducted to ensure
compliance with the standard protocol (PRISMA). In terms of contributions, current research on the relationship between light
environment and subjective perception, physiological indicators, and cognitive performance has been refined. This paper briefly
summarized the practical strategies to improve the light environment in indoor places. Additionally, the paper discusses potential
improvements and development directions. This study has practical significance for improving indoor light environment, living
standard and learning/working quality.
5.1. Discussion
In this study, we focused on two aspects of the light environment: illuminance and CCT. We analyzed 122 articles to summarize the
research findings. This paper found discrepancies in results across various studies and delves into the factors influencing these dif-
ferences. These factors are grouped into three main categories: the interplay between lighting elements, experimental conditions, and
responses from organisms.
There was a significant effect of illuminance and relevant CCT on both comfort and cognitive performance. Additionally, there was
a significant interaction effect of these factors [6,67]. The optimal illuminance and performance choices of subjects varied across
different color temperature environments. For instance, Lee et al. [6] demonstrated that subjects favored 500 lx at 6500 K, and 500 lx
and 750 lx at 4000 K. Various combinations of illumination impacted students’ cognition [124]. For attentional, 300 lx +6500 K was
found to be the most effective, while other combinations like 500 lx +6500 K, 300 lx +3000 K, and 100 lx +6500 K also improved
cognitive performance similarly. It is evident that the interaction among elements of the lighting environment significantly influences
the optimization of human psychology and cognition, leading to diverse research findings. However, further exploration and opti-
mization of these lighting combinations are necessary, especially considering the energy expenses in office and educational settings.
During the experimental setup, conditions were not consistent for many of the indicators studied, which contributed to some of the
differences in results. For example, Keis et al. [13] used CCT settings of 3000K, 3500K, and 5500K to represent low and high intensity,

could lead to varying results even in similar environmental settings. Tasks requiring different levels of illumination, as well as task
complexity and difficulty levels [100], can influence experimental outcomes. The limitation of experimental conditions results in the
inability of individual studies to achieve complete consistency in their results. However, this lack of consistency typically does not
significantly affect the overall summarized experimental results, especially within a specific range of indicators.
Certainly, feedback from the organism cannot be ignored. Studies have shown that light affects cognitive performance through both
visual and non-visual (circadian system) pathways [125]. Light exposure can affect mental states, influencing cognitive performance
through psychological responses [126]. In addition, light stimulation of ipRGCs increases sympathetic nervous system activity and
generates neuroendocrine responses (secretion of hormones such as melatonin and cortisol) [18,21], which regulate sleep, health, and
alertness, thereby affecting cognitive performance through physiological feedback [127]. The organism, which consists of physio-
logical and psychological components, is heterogeneous and subject to the influence of the first two factors, thus contributing to some
extent to the differences in experimental results. However, the exact impact is not yet fully understood and requires further
investigation.
5.2. Summary
1. Under the premise of meeting the basic lighting comfort conditions, subjective comfort evaluation will increase with higher
illuminance. However, visual comfort does not increase linearly, but shows a “diminishing returns” trend. Similarly subjective
comfort increases with higher CCT, but comfort at neutral CCT has an absolute advantage. In addition, the interaction between
illuminance and CCT is unavoidable in practical applications. Conditions of high illuminance and low CCT are undesirable.
Therefore, excessively high or low illuminance and CCT values should be avoided in the lighting design of a venue. Also, more
appropriate lighting conditions should be selected by combining the lighting preferences of the active scene and the interaction
between CCT and illuminance. In addition, high illuminance conditions have a moderating effect on positive mood and can also
reduce subjective sleepiness and subjective fatigue. Therefore, this finding may provide some references for improving students’
study performance and workers’ task performance. For example, lighting could be enhanced at specific times in the morning or
after the lunch break.
2. In terms of physiology, current studies mainly focus on melatonin, body temperature, heart rate, and EEG. Higher illuminance and
CCT present more active physiological manifestations (increased melatonin suppression, elevated body temperature, elevated heart
rate, and significant EEG changes). Both high illuminance and high CCT increase melatonin suppression, so they should be avoided
in nighttime lighting regimens to minimize the effects of light on circadian rhythms and sleep quality. High illuminance and high
CCT can activate the brain to some extent and increase motivation. However, high illuminance and CCT can also increase stress and
stress reactions, which is not good for human health. Therefore, the appropriate lighting conditions should be selected to avoid
physiological burden in the lighting design.
3. Cognitive performance also improves with higher illuminance and CCT. However, high illuminance and high CCT do not benefit all
cognitive performance. Similar to the subjective evaluation, some task tests have a threshold for improving the light environment
and are not the same. Different cognitive performance requires different lighting conditions. But opting for the neutral CCT
(3300K–5300K) for enhancing cognitive performance improvement doesn’t seem to go wrong. Therefore, it is necessary to design
personalized lighting schemes for specific places. Interactions between illuminance and CCT and between different environmental
factors also need to be considered.
4. There is a correlation between subjective perception, physiological indicators and cognitive performance. A comfortable lighting
condition can lead to a greater willingness to learn and contribute to cognitive performance. Light stimulation produces a series of
physiological responses that impact cognition and health. On the contrary, physiological indicators can be used as an objective and
powerful parameter to assist in verifying comfort and cognitive performance.
5. The interaction between illuminance and CCT cannot be ignored. This interaction is not only manifested in the influence of visual
comfort, but also in the improvement of cognitive performance and even changes in physiological indicators. For example, it has
been shown that both high illuminance and high CCT enhance the suppression of melatonin. This can have adverse effects on
circadian rhythms as well as sleep quality. At the same time, cognitive performance is relatively better under conditions of high
illuminance and high CCT. By utilizing the interaction of illuminance and CCT, then, we could theoretically achieve a double win of
enhanced cognitive performance and improved sleep quality.
5.3. Limitations
1. The review revealed that most of the existing studies are laboratory studies. The duration of exposure is controlled within 2h and
there are some limitations on the duration of light exposure. There are fewer studies on the effects of using artificial lighting in
classrooms as well as offices for long periods of time. In particular, the effects of light on physiological parameters under prolonged
exposure are not yet known.
2. The studies of illuminance and CCT on human physiological indices are reviewed. Existing articles mainly focus on the changes in
physiological indices brought about by lighting, but the related physiological mechanisms behind the effects of lighting are less
involved.

3. Among the literature on the effects of light, 70.5 % of the literature, totaling 101 articles, studied two or more of subjective feelings,
physiological indicators, and cognitive performance at the same time. However, the literature did not explore the interrelationship
among the three in depth, and the inner mechanism and physiological mechanism were not deeply discussed.
5.4. Future research
Summarizing the existing studies reveals unclear or insufficient research. Therefore, further research should focus on the following
points:
1. The effects of long-term exposure to light on people should be further studied. The exposure duration in existing studies is limited to
some extent. However, classrooms and offices are long-used spaces, and the influence of light in a short period is not absolutely
representative. People’s perception of the scene is not completely consistent with the standard indicators of modern environmental
or architectural lighting [128]. In particular, the influence of light on physiological parameters under long-term exposure is worthy
of further investigation.
2. More attention can be paid to the physiological mechanisms behind the effects of light and the intrinsic connection between
multiple evaluation indicators. A large part of the research contains three aspects: subjective evaluation, physiological indicators
and cognitive performance. However, the discussion of the results is more inclined to analyze these three aspects individually.
However, the three aspects of subjective, physiological and cognitive are interconnected. Therefore, it is necessary to strengthen
the exploration of the internal connection among the three aspects. In addition, due to the significant individual variability in
physiological metrics and cognitive performance, it is also possible to emphasize personalized lighting solutions supported by
different physiological metrics such as EEG signals [129].
3. It is necessary to establish a unified evaluation standard. In the current study, visual comfort can be achieved with low illuminance
and moderate CCT. There is a gap in these two areas. In addition, whether the physiological effects of light will endanger health also
needs to be considered. Based on this, it is necessary to consider the three aspects of subjective perception, physiological health and
cognitive performance. However, there is no conclusion about the comprehensive influence of light environment and the three
aspects, and the proportion of the three aspects cannot be determined. If there is a unified research method and evaluation in-
dicator, it may greatly promote these kinds of research. Therefore, the methods used in this field can be standardized in subsequent
studies. The same test content, results evaluation methods, and statistical analysis methods applied to past or contemporaneous
studies should be sought. In this way, the research results can be directly compared, and more accurate quantitative comprehensive
conclusions can be obtained.
4. Future studies should comprehensively explore the co-action of multiple factors. In studies that control for a single variable, the
effects of illuminance and CCT on subjective perception and physiology, respectively, are more accurately understood. Illuminance
and CCT often influence each other or one party dominates. But in some light conditions, existing research does not support it.
Therefore, more attention should be paid to the interaction of multiple light factors. In addition, in the real scene, people will be
affected by sound, light, heat and other factors. Moreover, studies have shown that there is an interaction between environmental
factors. In real scenarios, people are simultaneously exposed to acoustic, light, and thermal factors. For example, some buildings
improve the thermal environment by using shading nets, but this can also weaken indoor lighting [130]. It has been shown that
there are interactions between environmental factors, and it is crucial to balance the relationship among the various indoor
environmental factors. Therefore, the interaction between multiple environmental factors needs to be paid attention to in future
studies.
5. Expand your research into extreme environments. The light index involved in the experiment scene is visible in daily life, and the
research on extreme environment is rarely involved. The existing conclusions are not applicable to extreme light environment. For
example, the effects of light on long-term climates of extreme cold and extreme heat are unknown. In addition, the rapid urban
renewal and expansion leads to the serious shortage of ground space resources and the rapid development of underground space.
Hu et al. [131] explored the effects of lighting and thermal factors on human comfort, work performance, and sick building
syndrome in underground spaces, which suggests new research avenues. Also, the extent to which existing findings can be applied
to lighting design in underground spaces is not yet fully understood.
